newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Truckers prevent return to normal in Buenaventura.
newsitem.headline: Truckers prevent return to normal in Buenaventura.

text.p: Truckers demanding "standby" payments for time lost during a nine-day dockworkers' strike in Colombia's main Pacific Coast port prevented work there from returning to normal Friday, authorities said.

Buenaventura dockworkers returned to work Friday morning, a day after winning a deal with shipowners and cargo handling operators that should more than double their wages and provide a host of job-related benefits, union officials said.

But about 100 truck drivers, caught up in the strike since last week, were refusing to allow their cargo to be unloaded until they received additional payment for time lost while the port was paralyzed.

Jose Rios, regional head of the overland cargo transporters' association in Buenaventura Colfecar, said no more than about 100 of the 280 trucks that have jammed the port since last week were affected by the drivers' virtual sitdown strike.

But he said it was a "serious problem" because there was no immediate indication who might be prepared to yield to the drivers' demands for compensation for the strike, which blocked about 60 percent of the country's coffee exports, all its sugar exports and more than half of Colombia's foreign trade.
Most of the trucks affected by the new labor problem were laden with coffee, Rios said.

Rios said he agreed with private coffee exporters who told Reuters they saw no reason that they should be the ones to cover the truckers' losses, since they had nothing to do with the cause of the port strike and were adversely affected by it just like everyone else.
In some cases, drivers were asking for add-on payments totalling up to $3,000 for their downtime in Buenaventura, Rios said.
A source at the National Coffee Growers' Federation said it was possible that the Federation would offer some form of compensation to settle the truckers' demands.

It was not immediately clear how soon the port would get back to its full operating capacity, however, and coffee exporters said they ran the risk of missing two ships that were set to steam out of the port later Friday.
